items.title: Big Tech Q3 2026 earnings — the full three-print picture: Microsoft (Oct 28) beat and surged on Azure +48% with capex of $39.4B coming in BELOW the ~$50B expected; Alphabet (Oct 28) beat on $127.6B revenue and 103% Cloud growth but fell ~8% on $51.4B capex and EPS miss; Meta (Oct 29) beat revenue but was crushed on a $9.89B litigation charge and tumbled after narrowing 2026 capex to $135–145B; Amazon (Oct 29) printed AWS +39% to $46B and record 13.9% operating margin but fell 6–9% after hours on EPS miss and soft Q4 guide; four-hyperscaler 2026 capex now tracks ~$720B
items.summary: The four hyperscalers' Q3 2026 prints are now all in and the pattern is clearer than it was yesterday afternoon. Microsoft (Oct 28 after close) printed $92.3B revenue (+19%), Azure $33.2B (+48%, first time Microsoft disclosed the dollar figure, above its own ~45% guide), Microsoft Cloud $63.9B (+30%), net income $36.6B (+32%), and capex of $39.4B — materially BELOW the ~$50B the market expected — on a $175B calendar-2026 capex guide held unchanged from July; shares rose roughly 8% after hours. Alphabet (Oct 28 after close) printed $127.6B revenue (+25%) with Google Cloud up 103% YoY to $30.7B and Cloud operating margin expanding from 23.7% to 36.2%, but net income fell to ~$26.2B on equity-investment losses, Q3 capex hit $51.4B producing roughly negative $9.1B free cash flow, EPS of $2.12 missed consensus near $3.00, and shares dropped about 8% in after-hours trading. Meta (Oct 29 after close) printed $64.6B revenue versus $63.3B expected but GAAP EPS came in at $3.83 versus $6.67 expected on a $9.89B litigation charge; Q3 capex was $34.9B with negative FCF of about $2.12B, and the company narrowed 2026 capex guidance to $135–145B (from $130–145B) while guiding 'notably larger' AI investments in 2027. Amazon (Oct 29 after close, which the Oct 30 digest hadn't fully absorbed) reported AWS revenue of ~$46B (+39% YoY, the fastest AWS growth in 18 quarters), AWS operating income of $17.8B at a 38.7% margin, an AWS backlog of $578B (triple-digit YoY growth), and Andy Jassy saying AWS growth is projected to exceed 40% in both 2027 and 2028 — but overall EPS came in at $1.89 vs ~$1.96 expected, Q4 revenue guidance of $240–247B landed below estimates, trailing FCF fell to roughly negative $42.4B, and the stock dropped 6–9% in extended trading. Combined 2026 capex: Alphabet ~$180–190B, Microsoft ~$175B, Meta $135–145B, Amazon ~$220B — four-hyperscaler calendar-2026 total of roughly $720B, up from $410B in 2025. Apple reports fiscal Q4 2026 on Monday November 2 at 2:00 PM PT; the quarter covers iPhone 18 Pro's launch week. Apple guided 9–11% YoY revenue growth, implying roughly $111.7–$113.7B against the $102.5B base from Q4 2025, down from the 16% Q3 print. Siri AI launched in English with iOS 27 on September 14; whether it drove any upgrade-cycle bump in iPhone 18 Pro launch-week sales is the central narrative on the November 2 call.
items.why_it_matters: The three-print picture is sharper and in one specific way different from where the Oct 30 pm digest left it. The Oct 30 pm framing — 'the market just stopped looking through hyperscaler AI spending the way it did two quarters ago' — only holds for three of the four hyperscalers. Microsoft is the exception, and the exception is diagnostic: Microsoft reported $39.4B in capex against a market-expectation of roughly $50B, held its $175B calendar-2026 capex guide unchanged, and the stock surged ~8% after hours. The pattern that fits all four prints together is more specific: hyperscalers are being rewarded for capex that comes in UNDER guide-and-expectation, and punished for capex that overshoots guide-and-expectation or that fails to translate to the bottom line. Alphabet overshot on capex ($51.4B vs guide implying lower per-quarter pacing) and missed on EPS; Meta had an EPS blowup from a one-off litigation charge plus a 'notably larger' 2027 capex signal; Amazon had the strongest AI-business signal of any of the four (AWS +39%, $578B backlog, 40%+ guide for 2027 and 2028) but missed on EPS and soft-guided Q4 — the AI story is working but the overall-company numbers aren't yet. For a hobbyist Python coder, three practical implications tighten with this update. First, the Microsoft print is the one that most directly affects developer-tier pricing: Microsoft is the hyperscaler most aligned with OpenAI's API economics and the Azure OpenAI pricing, and Microsoft holding capex-under-expected while printing 48% Azure growth means the pressure to raise developer-tier prices is lower from Microsoft than from Alphabet or Amazon for now. Second, the AWS backlog of $578B with 40%+ growth guided for the next two years is the single clearest signal that enterprise AI demand is durable at scale — AWS is more expensive than most alternatives for inference-heavy workloads, so this is a stronger demand signal than price-sensitive consumer pricing changes would be. Third, the Oct 30 pm digest's specific prediction — 'if three of four hyperscalers get punished for capex this cycle, the odds that one of them (likely Meta) trims the top end of its 2027 guide in January goes up' — now looks very likely to play out; three of the four did get punished, and Meta's 'notably larger' 2027 signal is the one most likely to see pressure to walk back in the January call. Specific numbers to watch over the next week: (a) Apple's Nov 2 print at 2:00 PM PT — guidance is 9–11% YoY (~$111.7–$113.7B), the quarter includes iPhone 18 Pro launch-week sales, and the central question is whether Siri AI (English, iOS 27, September 14 rollout) shows up in Services or units; (b) any walk-back of Meta's 'notably larger' 2027 framing in follow-up analyst calls; (c) whether Microsoft converts the capex-under-expected framing into a sustained outperformance, which would be the test of whether the market is actually using capex discipline as the sorting signal rather than reacting to EPS surprises specifically.
items.why_it_matters_brief: All four hyperscalers now reported — Microsoft surged on capex coming in below the $50B expected, the other three sold off. Capex-discipline, not capex-level, is the market's new sorting signal.

items.title: OpenAI reportedly plans to buy Google TPUs — update: a 16-hour overnight window produced no new primary confirmation; Alphabet's Oct 28 earnings call did not call out an OpenAI-specific TPU customer by name, OpenAI and Google both still silent, and the single-source nature of the original report remains the main caveat
items.summary: The Information reported on October 27, 2026 — and Reuters and multiple secondary outlets picked it up on Oct 27–28 — that OpenAI is preparing to purchase Google TPU chips rather than only renting TPU capacity through Google Cloud. The overnight window since the Oct 30 pm digest produced no new primary confirmation: Alphabet reported Q3 2026 on Oct 28 after close and the prepared remarks and release did not call out an OpenAI-specific TPU deal, OpenAI has not published any TPU-related technical post or benchmark, and the single-anonymous-source nature of the original scoop remains the main caveat. Supporting evidence from the original reporting still stands: OpenAI has posted job listings for engineers to tune its models for TPU hardware, OpenAI already began using rented Google TPU capacity in mid-2025, and TrendForce separately reports Oracle plans to bring TPUs into its cloud offering in 2027 (which would be the first time Google's TPU hardware is sold outside Google Cloud at scale). Volume, price, and timeline are not disclosed in the report.
items.why_it_matters: The clearest signal yet that the AI-chip buy-side is actively trying to diversify away from Nvidia's near-monopoly on frontier training and inference — and the 16-hour overnight window since the Oct 30 pm digest sharpens one specific thing: Alphabet had the natural venue to confirm an OpenAI deal on its Oct 28 earnings call and chose not to. That's not a disconfirmation, but it is a datum. Google's Q3 Cloud growth printing at 103% YoY (per the Big Tech earnings item in this snapshot) means Google doesn't need to name-check a specific hyperscaler-tier customer to make the Cloud narrative work — but companies routinely do call out marquee TPU wins when they have them, and this one would have been the biggest in TPU history. For Gabe's Python stack specifically, the practical implications are a step removed but worth tracking: (1) PyTorch's XLA/TPU backend has been stable but second-class since the Google-TPU-via-Colab era — if OpenAI is tuning models for TPUs, the quality of the open-source Python toolchain for 'write PyTorch, run on TPU' goes up because that's exactly what OpenAI's engineers will have to improve to make their own work ship, which usually leaks back into open-source libraries like torch_xla and JAX; (2) if TPUs become a credible second supplier at the frontier, the per-token cost floor on inference goes down over 2027–2028 because the top labs can play Nvidia and Google against each other on compute pricing, and some of that will show up as cheaper API tokens; (3) the Oracle-TPUs-in-2027 angle, if real, is the one that matters for anyone who builds on top of multiple clouds, because it would be the first time a TPU-tuned model you could call from a non-Google cloud exists. Caveats worth carrying: the primary report rests on a single anonymous source per The Information, neither OpenAI nor Google has confirmed as of this run, and OpenAI's earlier public framing — 'early-stage testing, no broad use' — has not been formally retracted. The 'TPU is easier said than done' point from TechRadar also remains real — OpenAI's codebase is deeply tuned to CUDA, and 'swapping chips' involves rewriting training/inference stacks in ways that routinely take 6–18 months even for well-resourced teams. Specific numbers to watch over the next 4–8 weeks: (a) whether Google or OpenAI publishes anything that would count as primary confirmation; (b) whether Oracle's rumored 2027 TPU rollout gets its own primary-source announcement from Oracle; (c) whether the next Information story adds a second source or specifics on volume and timeline.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 open weights — overnight update: additional independent-ish benchmark data points surface: Vals AI overall index places Large 4 35th of 48 at 48.1%, LMArena crowd leaderboard had it 112th as of mid-October, and Mistral's own-run Surge AI blind coding eval put the preview at 3.74/5 (2nd of 5, behind Opus 5's 4.22); list pricing is $1.36/M input tokens with a launch discount to $0.68
items.summary: The Oct 30 pm digest put Mistral Large 4 at Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 38 (vs 9 for Large 3, 58–59 for the frontier closed models) and surfaced the 524K-vs-claimed-1M context-window gap. Overnight: a few additional data points add detail without changing the mid-pack-not-frontier framing. (1) Vals AI's overall index — a different composite than the Harvey Legal Agent benchmark where Large 4 ranked 6th of 75 at 15.83% — places Large 4 at 35th of 48 at 48.1%. (2) LMArena's crowd-voted text leaderboard had Large 4 at 112th as of October 13 (a pre-weight-release ranking that will likely move as more users rate the open-weight version). (3) The Mistral-published Surge AI blind coding evaluation — not fully independent since the harness was run by Mistral — put the Large 4 preview at 3.74/5, second of five models tested, behind Claude Opus 5 at 4.22. (4) Pricing: list input is $1.36 per million tokens with a launch discount to $0.68 per million (Mistral's own hosted-API pricing, separate from the self-hosted open-weight path). (5) Independent reproduction of the 81.7% reproduce-and-patch cybersecurity score is confirmed on Artificial Analysis. The HuggingFace listing, the 4× B200/B300 inference hardware requirement, the ~524K vs claimed 1M practical context window, and the vLLM/SGLang Python inference path from the am and pm all remain accurate.
items.why_it_matters: The overnight data points sharpen the pm digest's framing without changing it: Mistral Large 4 is a credible open-weight contender that is clearly a step up from Large 3 on the same measurement framework (Artificial Analysis Index 38 vs 9), but it is not at the frontier of what the closed labs currently ship. The two useful overnight additions for Gabe: (1) the Vals-overall 48.1% / 35th-of-48 placement is a composite datum that lines up with the mid-pack framing from the pm — strong in specific domains (cybersecurity reproduce-and-patch 81.7%; Harvey Legal Agent 6th of 75) and middling on a general-purpose composite. (2) The $1.36/M input list price with a $0.68 launch discount is a specific number worth knowing because it quantifies the Mistral-hosted-API cost against the self-hosted open-weight path — if Gabe wanted to try the model, calling the Mistral API at $0.68/M input tokens (while the launch discount lasts) is roughly ~10x cheaper than renting the 4× B200/B300 hardware for self-hosting, so unless there's a specific reason to self-host (license, data residency, latency), the hosted API is the right starting point this month. The useful framing hasn't changed from the pm: Large 4 is 'the open-weight model that's good enough to run yourself when a frontier closed-API call isn't the right tradeoff,' not 'the open-weight model that replaces GPT or Claude for complex work.' The 524K vs 1M context-window gap, the DeepSWE 61.7% agentic-coding figure not being independently reproducible, and the vLLM-and-SGLang Python inference path all still stand. The LMArena 112th ranking is the one data point most likely to change in the next 2–4 weeks as users rate the open-weight version in the arena; worth watching if Gabe wants to see where crowd preference lands.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Vals-overall 48.1% (35th of 48) and $0.68/M launch pricing confirm the mid-pack-not-frontier read — the hosted API is cheaper than self-hosting unless license or data-residency rules it out.
